image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Alluvial / flow-style area chart** with **variable-width bands** over time.
- It also functions like a **stacked area chart** within the tan “unemployed” region, showing subcategories.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Stacking**: The tan “Total unemployed” area is subdivided into stacked subgroups (“Temporarily laid off,” “Other,” “Permanently laid off”).
- **Side-by-side grouped areas**: A separate purple area (“Not in labor force but want a job”) is shown adjacent to the tan unemployed area.
- **Temporal layout**: Values are shown across a vertical time axis from **Jan.** to **April** to **Sept.**
- **Direct labeling**: Categories are labeled inside the shapes rather than using a legend.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (Jan., April, Sept.) | Temporal | Position on vertical axis |
| Number of people / count (millions) | Quantitative | Width/area of each band; numeric labels at right |
| Labor force status group (“Total unemployed”, “Not in labor force but want a job”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate colored regions; direct text labels |
| Unemployed subgroup (“Temporarily laid off”, “Other”, “Permanently laid off”) | Categorical/nominal | Stacked subdivisions within tan area; internal boundaries; direct text labels |
| Millions labels (12 million, 32 million, 19 million) | Quantitative | Text annotation |
raw_comment:
I noticed that the number of people who were unemployed at the beginning of the year was 12 million. There was a peak in unemployment in April at 32 million, but it has decreased to 19 million as of September. More people were temporarily laid off than those who were permanently laid off. The number of people looking for employment (purple region) seems to match the total number unemployed (beige region). 
I wonder what the most significant factor in unemployment was. Obviously, the pandemic greatly affected the unemployment rate, but did most people become unemployed because workplace shut down entirely or because of budgeting that took place as a result from the pandemic? I wonder which kinds of jobs had the most lay-offs and which had the least. In addition, I wonder how it would look if unemployment was charted geographically. I wonder how many businesses will be able to rehire temporarily laid off employees or if those businesses will end up shutting down completely. I also wonder if those who chose to leave their jobs will remain unemployed or will go back to work again. 
This impacts my community because I know people have been laid off, and unemployment affects a family's socioeconomic status, which also ends up affecting things like healthcare, food, and housing. In addition, more small businesses have been affected than large businesses. 

A headline could be "Unemployment Spikes Following the Pandemic: Will Things Ever Go Back to Normal?"

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph shows the composition of the American unemployed workers from Jan. until Sept. 2020.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Plus, share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in the graph. 

What’s most interesting and often surprising in investigating a graph is when you compare different groups in a graph, such as temporarily laid off workers to permanently laid off workers.  Or, January unemployed (before the pandemic) to September unemployed.  What insightful comparison can you make?

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these visual representations and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Keep noticing and wondering.  There will be no release next week because Nov. 11 is the Veteran’s Day holiday.  Our next graph will be released by Friday, November 13.  Stay tuned for a fun graph that has something to do with Thanksgiving.

## 1) Chart type
- **Alluvial / flow-style area chart** with **variable-width bands** over time.
- It also functions like a **stacked area chart** within the tan “unemployed” region, showing subcategories.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Stacking**: The tan “Total unemployed” area is subdivided into stacked subgroups (“Temporarily laid off,” “Other,” “Permanently laid off”).
- **Side-by-side grouped areas**: A separate purple area (“Not in labor force but want a job”) is shown adjacent to the tan unemployed area.
- **Temporal layout**: Values are shown across a vertical time axis from **Jan.** to **April** to **Sept.**
- **Direct labeling**: Categories are labeled inside the shapes rather than using a legend.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (Jan., April, Sept.) | Temporal | Position on vertical axis |
| Number of people / count (millions) | Quantitative | Width/area of each band; numeric labels at right |
| Labor force status group (“Total unemployed”, “Not in labor force but want a job”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate colored regions; direct text labels |
| Unemployed subgroup (“Temporarily laid off”, “Other”, “Permanently laid off”) | Categorical/nominal | Stacked subdivisions within tan area; internal boundaries; direct text labels |
| Millions labels (12 million, 32 million, 19 million) | Quantitative | Text annotation |

## 1) Chart type

- It also functions like a **stacked area chart** within the tan “unemployed” region, showing subcategories.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Stacking**: The tan “Total unemployed” area is subdivided into stacked subgroups (“Temporarily laid off,” “Other,” “Permanently laid off”).
- **Side-by-side grouped areas**: A separate purple area (“Not in labor force but want a job”) is shown adjacent to the tan unemployed area.
- **Temporal layout**: Values are shown across a vertical time axis from **Jan.** to **April** to **Sept.**
- **Direct labeling**: Categories are labeled inside the shapes rather than using a legend.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Time (Jan., April, Sept.) | Temporal | Position on vertical axis |
| Number of people / count (millions) | Quantitative | Width/area of each band; numeric labels at right |
| Labor force status group (“Total unemployed”, “Not in labor force but want a job”) | Categorical/nominal | Separate colored regions; direct text labels |
| Unemployed subgroup (“Temporarily laid off”, “Other”, “Permanently laid off”) | Categorical/nominal | Stacked subdivisions within tan area; internal boundaries; direct text labels |
| Millions labels (12 million, 32 million, 19 million) | Quantitative | Text annotation |

|---|---|---|
